{{Short description|Mathematical theory about infinitely iterated function composition}}

In [[mathematics]], '''infinite [[Function composition|composition]]s of [[analytic function]]s (ICAF)''' offer alternative formulations of [[Generalized continued fraction|analytic continued fractions]], [[series (mathematics)|series]], [[product (mathematics)|products]] and other infinite expansions, and the theory evolving from such compositions may shed light on the [[limit of a sequence| convergence/divergence]] of these expansions. Some functions can actually be expanded directly as infinite compositions. In addition, it is possible to use ICAF to evaluate solutions of [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] equations involving infinite expansions. [[Complex dynamics]] offers another venue for [[iterated function system|iteration of systems of functions]] rather than a single function. For infinite compositions of a ''single function'' see [[Iterated function]]. For compositions of a finite number of functions, useful in [[fractal]] theory, see [[Iterated function system]].

Although the title of this article specifies analytic functions, there are results for more general [[Complex analysis|functions of a complex variable]] as well.

==Notation==
There are several notations describing infinite compositions, including the following:

'''Forward compositions:''' <math>F_{k,n}(z) = f_k \circ f_{k + 1} \circ \dots \circ f_{n - 1} \circ f_n (z).</math>

'''Backward compositions:''' <math>G_{k,n}(z) = f_n \circ f_{n - 1} \circ \dots \circ f_{k + 1} \circ f_k (z).</math>

In each case convergence is interpreted as the existence of the following limits:

:<math> \lim_{n\to \infty} F_{1,n}(z), \qquad \lim_{n\to\infty} G_{1,n}(z).</math>

For convenience, set {{math|''F<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') {{=}} ''F''<sub>1,''n''</sub>(''z'')}} and {{math|''G<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') {{=}} ''G''<sub>1,''n''</sub>(''z'')}}.

One may also write <math>F_n(z)=\underset{k=1}{\overset{n}{\mathop R}}\,f_k(z)=f_1 \circ f_2\circ \cdots \circ f_n(z)</math>  and
<math>G_n(z)=\underset{k=1}{\overset{n}{\mathop L}}\,g_k(z)=g_n \circ g_{n-1}\circ \cdots \circ g_1(z)</math>

'''Comment''': It is not clear when the first explorations of infinite compositions of analytic functions not restricted to sequences of functions of a specific kind occurred. Possibly in the 1980s. <ref>{{cite journal |last=Gill |first=John |title=Compositions of analytic functions of the form Fn(z)=Fn-1(fn(z)),fn->f |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |date=1988 |volume=23 |pages=179-184 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0377042788902798}}</ref> 

==Contraction theorem==
Many results can be considered extensions of the following result:

{{math theorem|name=Contraction Theorem for Analytic Functions<ref>{{cite book |first=P. |last=Henrici |title=Applied and Computational Complex Analysis |volume=1 |publisher=Wiley |orig-date=1974 |isbn=978-0-471-60841-7 |date=1988 |url={{GBurl|ZrJ6GX5a2WMC|pg=PR13}}}}</ref>|math_statement= Let ''f'' be analytic in a simply-connected region ''S'' and continuous on the closure {{overline|''S''}} of ''S''. Suppose ''f''({{overline|''S''}}) is a bounded set contained in ''S''. Then for all ''z'' in {{overline|''S''}} there exists an [[attractive fixed point]] α of ''f'' in ''S'' such that:
<math display="block">F_n(z)=(f\circ f\circ \cdots \circ f)(z)\to \alpha.</math>}}

==Infinite compositions of contractive functions==
Let {''f<sub>n</sub>''} be a sequence of functions analytic on a simply-connected domain ''S''. Suppose there exists a compact set Ω ⊂ ''S'' such that for each ''n'', ''f<sub>n</sub>''(''S'') ⊂ Ω.

{{math theorem|name=Forward (inner or right) Compositions Theorem|math_statement= {''F<sub>n</sub>''} converges uniformly on compact subsets of ''S'' to a constant function ''F''(''z'') = ''λ''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lorentzen |first1=Lisa |title=Compositions of contractions |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |date=November 1990 |volume=32 |issue=1–2 |pages=169–178 |doi=10.1016/0377-0427(90)90428-3 |doi-access=free }}</ref> }}

{{math theorem|name=Backward (outer or left) Compositions Theorem|math_statement= {''G<sub>n</sub>''} converges uniformly on compact subsets of ''S'' to ''γ'' ∈ Ω if and only if the sequence of fixed points {''γ<sub>n</sub>''} of the {''f<sub>n</sub>''} converges to ''γ''.<ref name = Gilla>{{cite journal |first=J. |last=Gill |title=The use of the sequence F<sub>n</sub>(z)=f<sub>n</sub>∘⋯∘f<sub>1</sub>(z) in computing the fixed points of continued fractions, products, and series |journal=Appl. Numer. Math. |volume=8 |issue=6 |pages=469–476 |date=1991 |doi=10.1016/0168-9274(91)90109-D |url=}}</ref>}}

Additional theory resulting from investigations based on these two theorems, particularly Forward Compositions Theorem, include location analysis for the limits obtained in the following reference.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Keen|first1=Linda|first2=Nikola|last2=Lakic|title=Accumulation constants of iterated function systems with Bloch target domains.|journal=Annales Academiae Scientiarum Fennicae Mathematica|volume= 32|number= 1|publisher= Finnish Academy of Science and Letters|location=Helsinki|year=2007|url=https://www.maths.tcd.ie/EMIS/journals/AASF/Vol32/KeenLakic.html}}</ref> For a different approach to Backward Compositions Theorem, see the following reference.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Keen|first1=Linda|first2=Nikola|last2=Lakic|chapter=Forward iterated function systems|url=http://comet.lehman.cuny.edu/keenl/forwarditer.pdf|pages=292–299 |editor-last=Jiang |editor-first=Yunping |title=Complex dynamics and related topics: lectures from the Morningside Center of Mathematics |date=2003 |publisher=International Press |editor-first2=Yuefei|editor-last2=Wang |isbn=1-57146-121-3 |location=Sommerville |oclc=699694753}}</ref>

Regarding Backward Compositions Theorem, the example ''f''<sub>2''n''</sub>(''z'') = 1/2 and ''f''<sub>2''n''−1</sub>(''z'') = −1/2 for ''S'' = {''z'' : |''z''| < 1} demonstrates the inadequacy of simply requiring contraction into a compact subset, like Forward Compositions Theorem.

For functions not necessarily analytic the [[Contraction mapping|Lipschitz]] condition suffices:

{{math theorem|name=Theorem<ref name=Gillb>{{cite journal |first=J. |last=Gill |title=A Primer on the Elementary Theory of Infinite Compositions of Complex Functions |journal=Communications in the Analytic Theory of Continued Fractions |volume=XXIII |date=2017 |url=https://www.coloradomesa.edu/math-stat/catcf/papers/primerinfcompcomplexfcns.pdf}}</ref> |math_statement=Suppose <math>S</math> is a simply connected compact subset of <math>\Complex</math> and let <math>t_n : S \to S</math> be a family of functions that satisfies 
<math display="block"> \forall n, \forall z_1, z_2 \in S, \exists \rho: \quad \left|t_n(z_1)-t_n(z_2) \right|\le \rho |z_1-z_2|, \quad \rho < 1.</math>
Define:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
G_n(z) &= \left (t_n\circ t_{n-1}\circ \cdots \circ t_1 \right ) (z) \\
F_n(z) &= \left (t_1 \circ t_2\circ \cdots \circ t_n \right ) (z)
\end{align}</math>
Then <math>F_n(z)\to \beta \in S</math> uniformly on <math>S.</math> If <math>\alpha_n</math> is the unique fixed point of <math>t_n</math> then <math>G_n(z)\to \alpha </math> uniformly on <math>S</math> if and only if <math>|\alpha_n -\alpha| = \varepsilon_n \to 0</math>.}}

==Infinite compositions of other functions==

=== Non-contractive complex functions ===
Results involving '''[[entire function]]s''' include the following, as examples. Set

:<math>\begin{align}
f_n(z)&=a_n z + c_{n,2}z^2+c_{n,3} z^3+\cdots \\
\rho_n &= \sup_r \left\{ \left| c_{n,r} \right|^{\frac{1}{r-1}} \right\}
\end{align}</math>

Then the following results hold:

{{math theorem|name=Theorem E1<ref name=Kojima>{{cite journal |last1=Kojima |first1=Shota |title=On the convergence of infinite compositions of entire functions |journal=Archiv der Mathematik |date=May 2012 |volume=98 |issue=5 |pages=453–465 |doi=10.1007/s00013-012-0385-z |s2cid=121444171 }}</ref> |math_statement= If ''a<sub>n</sub>'' ≡ 1,
<math display="block">\sum_{n=1}^\infty \rho_n < \infty</math>
then ''F<sub>n</sub>'' → ''F'' is entire.}}

{{math theorem|name=Theorem E2<ref name=Gillc>{{cite journal |first=J. |last=Gill |title=Convergence of Infinite Compositions of Complex Functions |journal=Communications in the Analytic Theory of Continued Fractions |volume=XIX |date=2012 |url=https://www.coloradomesa.edu/math-stat/documents/JohnGillResearchnoteInfiniteCompositions2.pdf}}</ref>|math_statement= Set ''ε''<sub>''n''</sub> = {{abs|''a<sub>n</sub>''−1}} suppose there exists non-negative ''δ''<sub>''n''</sub>, ''M''<sub>1</sub>, ''M''<sub>2</sub>, ''R'' such that the following holds:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \varepsilon_n &< \infty, \\
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \delta_n &< \infty, \\
\prod_{n=1}^\infty (1+\delta_n) &< M_1, \\
\prod_{n=1}^\infty (1+\varepsilon_n) &< M_2, \\
\rho_n &< \frac{\delta_n}{R M_1 M_2}.
\end{align}</math>
Then ''G<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') → ''G''(''z'') is analytic for {{abs|''z''}} < ''R''. Convergence is uniform on compact subsets of {''z'' : {{abs|''z''}} < ''R''}.}}

'''Additional elementary results include:'''

{{math theorem|name=Theorem GF3<ref name=Gillb /> |math_statement=Suppose <math>f_k(z)=z+\rho_k \varphi_k (z)</math> where there exist <math>R, M > 0</math> such that <math>|z| < R</math> implies <math>| \varphi_k (z)| < M, \forall k, \ </math> Furthermore, suppose <math display="inline">\rho_k \ge 0, \sum_{k=1}^\infty \rho_k < \infty </math> and  <math display="inline">R > M\sum_{k=1}^\infty \rho_k.</math> Then for <math display="inline">R* < R-M\sum_{k=1}^\infty \rho_k</math>
<math display="block">G_n(z)\equiv \left (f_n\circ f_{n-1}\circ \cdots \circ f_1 \right ) (z) \to G(z) \qquad  \text{ for } \{z:|z|<R*\}</math>}}

{{math theorem|name=Theorem GF4<ref name=Gillb /> |math_statement=Suppose <math>f_k(z)=z+\rho_k \varphi_k (z)</math> where there exist <math>R, M > 0</math> such that <math>|z|<R</math> and <math>|\zeta|<R</math> implies <math>|\varphi_k (z)| < M</math> and <math>|\varphi_k (z)-\varphi_k (\zeta)|\le  r|z-\zeta|, \forall k. \ </math> Furthermore, suppose <math display="inline">\rho_k\ge 0, \sum_{k=1}^\infty \rho_k < \infty </math> and <math display="inline">R>M \sum_{k=1}^\infty \rho_k.</math> Then for <math display="inline">R* < R-M\sum_{k=1}^\infty\rho_k</math>
<math display="block">F_n(z)\equiv \left (f_1\circ f_2\circ \cdots \circ f_n \right) (z) \to F(z) \qquad \text{ for } \{z:|z|< R* \}</math>}}

=== Linear fractional transformations ===
Results<ref name=Gillc /> for compositions of '''[[möbius transformation|linear fractional (Möbius) transformations]]''' include the following, as examples:

{{math theorem|name=Theorem LFT1|math_statement= On the set of convergence of a sequence {''F<sub>n</sub>''} of non-singular LFTs, the limit function is either:
<ol type="a">
<li>a non-singular LFT,</li>
<li>a function taking on two distinct values, or</li>
<li>a constant.</li>
</ol>
In (a), the sequence converges everywhere in the extended plane. In (b), the sequence converges either everywhere, and to the same value everywhere except at one point, or it converges at only two points. Case (c) can occur with every possible set of convergence.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Piranian |first1=G. |last2=Thron |first2=W. J. |title=Convergence properties of sequences of linear fractional transformations. |journal=Michigan Mathematical Journal |date=1957 |volume=4 |issue=2 |doi=10.1307/mmj/1028989001 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
}}

{{math theorem|name=Theorem LFT2<ref>{{cite journal |last1=de Pree |first1=J. D. |last2=Thron |first2=W. J. |title=On sequences of Moebius transformations |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift |date=December 1962 |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=184–193 |doi=10.1007/BF01162375 |s2cid=120487262 }}</ref> |math_statement= If {''F<sub>n</sub>''} converges to an LFT, then ''f<sub>n</sub>'' converge to the identity function ''f''(''z'') = ''z''.}}

{{math theorem|name=Theorem LFT3<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mandell |first1=Michael |last2=Magnus |first2=Arne |title=On convergence of sequences of linear fractional transformations |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift |date=1970 |volume=115 |issue=1 |pages=11–17 |doi=10.1007/BF01109744 |s2cid=119407993 }}</ref> |math_statement= If ''f<sub>n</sub>'' → ''f'' and all functions are ''hyperbolic'' or ''loxodromic'' Möbius transformations, then ''F<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') → ''λ'', a constant, for all <math display="inline">z \ne \beta = \lim_{n\to \infty} \beta_n</math>, where {''β<sub>n</sub>''} are the repulsive fixed points of the {''f<sub>n</sub>''}.}}

{{math theorem|name=Theorem LFT4<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gill |first1=John |title=Infinite compositions of Möbius transformations |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |date=1973 |volume=176 |pages=479 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1973-0316690-6 |doi-access=free }}</ref> |math_statement=If ''f<sub>n</sub>'' → ''f'' where ''f'' is ''parabolic'' with fixed point ''γ''. Let the fixed-points of the {''f<sub>n</sub>''} be {''γ''<sub>''n''</sub>} and {''β<sub>n</sub>''}. If
<math display="block">\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left|\gamma_n-\beta_n \right| < \infty \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{n=1}^\infty n \left|\beta_{n+1}-\beta_n \right|<\infty</math>
then ''F<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') → ''λ'', a constant in the extended complex plane, for all ''z''.}}

==Examples and applications==

=== Continued fractions ===
The value of the infinite continued fraction

:<math>\cfrac{a_1}{b_1+\cfrac{a_2}{b_2+\cdots}}</math>

may be expressed as the limit of the sequence {''F<sub>n</sub>''(0)} where

:<math>f_n(z)=\frac{a_n}{b_n+z}.</math>

As a simple example, a well-known result (Worpitsky's circle theorem<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Beardon | first = A. F.
 | doi = 10.1016/S0377-0427(00)00318-6
 | issue = 1–2
 | journal = Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics
 | mr = 1835708
 | pages = 143–148
 | title = Worpitzky's theorem on continued fractions
 | volume = 131
 | year = 2001| bibcode = 2001JCoAM.131..143B
 }}</ref>) follows from an application of Theorem (A):

Consider the continued fraction

:<math>\cfrac{a_1\zeta }{1+\cfrac{a_2\zeta }{1+\cdots}} </math>

with

:<math>f_n(z)=\frac{a_n \zeta }{1+z}.</math>

Stipulate that |ζ| < 1 and |''z''| < ''R'' < 1.  Then for 0 < ''r'' < 1,

: <math>|a_n|<rR(1-R)\Rightarrow \left|f_n(z) \right|<rR<R\Rightarrow \frac{a_1\zeta }{1+\frac{a_2\zeta }{1+\cdots}} = F(\zeta) </math>, analytic for |''z''| < 1. Set ''R'' = 1/2.

'''Example.''' <math>F(z)=\frac{(i-1)z}{1+i+z\text{   }+}\text{  }\frac{(2-i)z}{1+2i+z\text{   }+}\text{  }\frac{(3-i)z}{1+3i+z\text{   }+} \cdots, </math> <math>[-15,15]</math>
[[File:Continued fraction1.jpg|thumb|center|350px|Example: Continued fraction1 – Topographical (moduli) image of a continued fraction (one for each point) in the complex plane. [−15,15]]]

'''Example.'''<ref name=Gillc /> A ''fixed-point continued fraction form'' (a single variable).
:<math>f_{k,n}(z)=\frac{\alpha_{k,n} \beta_{k,n}}{\alpha_{k,n}+\beta_{k,n}-z}, \alpha_{k,n}=\alpha_{k,n}(z), \beta_{k,n}=\beta_{k,n}(z), F_n(z)= \left (f_{1,n} \circ\cdots \circ f_{n,n} \right ) (z)</math>
:<math>\alpha_{k,n}=x \cos(ty)+iy \sin(tx), \beta_{k,n}= \cos(ty)+i \sin(tx), t=k/n</math>

[[File:Infinite Brooch.jpg|thumb|center|370px|Example: Infinite Brooch - Topographical (moduli) image of a ''continued fraction form'' in the complex plane. (6<x<9.6),(4.8<y<8)]]

=== Direct functional expansion ===
Examples illustrating the conversion of a function directly into a composition follow:

'''Example 1.'''<ref name=Kojima /><ref>{{cite book |first=N. |last=Steinmetz |title=Rational Iteration |publisher=de Gruyter |orig-date=1993 |isbn=978-3-11-088931-4 |url={{GBurl|qZGWgVuGHiYC|pg=PR7}} |date=2011}}</ref> Suppose <math>\phi</math> is an entire function satisfying the following conditions:
:<math>\begin{cases} \phi (tz)=t\left( \phi (z)+\phi (z)^2 \right) & |t|> 1 \\ \phi(0) = 0 \\ \phi'(0) =1 \end{cases}</math>
Then 
:<math>f_n(z)=z+\frac{z^2}{t^n}\Longrightarrow F_n(z)\to \phi (z)</math>.

'''Example 2.'''<ref name=Kojima /> 
:<math>f_n(z)=z+\frac{z^2}{2^n}\Longrightarrow F_n(z)\to \frac{1}{2}\left( e^{2z}-1 \right)</math>

'''Example 3.'''<ref name=Gillb /> 
:<math>f_n(z)= \frac{z}{1-\tfrac{z^2}{4^n}}\Longrightarrow F_n(z)\to \tan (z)</math>

'''Example 4.'''<ref name=Gillb />
:<math>g_n(z)=\frac{2 \cdot 4^{n}}{z} \left ( \sqrt{1+\frac{z^2}{4^{n}}}-1 \right )\Longrightarrow G_n(z) \to \arctan (z)</math>

=== Calculation of fixed-points ===
Theorem (B) can be applied to determine the fixed-points of functions defined by infinite expansions or certain integrals. The following examples illustrate the process:

'''Example FP1.'''<ref name=Gilla /> For |''ζ''| ≤ 1 let

:<math>G(\zeta )=\frac{ \tfrac{e^\zeta}{4}}{3+\zeta +\cfrac{\tfrac{e^\zeta} 8 }{3+\zeta + \cfrac{\tfrac{e^\zeta}{12}}{3+\zeta +\cdots}}}</math>

To find α = ''G''(α), first we define:

:<math>\begin{align}
t_n(z)&=\cfrac{\tfrac{e^\zeta}{4n}}{3+\zeta +z} \\
f_n(\zeta )&= t_1\circ t_2\circ \cdots \circ t_n(0)
\end{align}</math>

Then calculate <math>G_n(\zeta )=f_n\circ \cdots \circ f_1(\zeta )</math> with ζ = 1, which gives: α = 0.087118118... to ten decimal places after ten iterations.

{{math theorem|name=Theorem FP2<ref name=Gillc />|math_statement=Let ''φ''(''ζ'', ''t'') be analytic in ''S'' = {''z'' : {{abs|''z''}} < ''R''} for all ''t'' in [0, 1] and continuous in ''t''. Set
<math display="block">f_n (\zeta)=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n \varphi \left( \zeta ,\tfrac{k}{n} \right).</math>
If {{abs|''φ''(''ζ'', ''t'')}} ≤ ''r'' < ''R'' for ''ζ'' ∈ ''S'' and ''t'' ∈ [0, 1], then
<math display="block">\zeta =\int_0^1 \varphi (\zeta ,t) \, dt</math>
has a unique solution, ''α'' in ''S'', with <math>\lim_{n\to \infty} G_n(\zeta ) = \alpha. </math>}}

=== Evolution functions ===
Consider a time interval, normalized to ''I'' = [0, 1]. ICAFs can be constructed to describe continuous motion of a point, ''z'', over the interval, but in such a way that at each "instant" the motion is virtually zero (see [[Zeno's paradoxes|Zeno's Arrow]]): For the interval divided into n equal subintervals, 1 ≤ ''k'' ≤ ''n'' set <math>g_{k,n}(z)=z+\varphi_{k,n}(z)</math> analytic or simply continuous – in a domain ''S'', such that

:<math>\lim_{n\to \infty}\varphi_{k,n}(z)=0</math> for all ''k'' and all ''z'' in ''S'', 
and <math>g_{k,n}(z) \in S</math>.

==== Principal example ====

Source:<ref name=Gillc />

:<math>\begin{align}
g_{k,n}(z) &=z+\frac{1}{n}\phi  \left (z,\tfrac{k}{n} \right ) \\
G_{k,n}(z) &= \left (g_{k,n}\circ g_{k-1,n} \circ \cdots \circ g_{1,n} \right ) (z) \\ 
G_n(z) &=G_{n,n}(z)
\end{align}</math>

implies

:<math>\lambda_n(z)\doteq G_n(z)-z=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \phi  \left( G_{k-1,n}(z)\tfrac k n \right)\doteq \frac 1 n \sum_{k=1}^n \psi \left (z,\tfrac{k}{n} \right) \sim \int_0^1 \psi (z,t)\,dt,</math>

where the integral is well-defined if <math>\tfrac{dz}{dt}=\phi (z,t)</math> has a closed-form solution ''z''(''t'').  Then

:<math>\lambda_n(z_0)\approx \int_0^1 \phi ( z(t),t)\,dt.</math>

Otherwise, the integrand is poorly defined although the value of the integral is easily computed. In this case one might call the integral a "virtual" integral.

'''Example.''' <math>\phi  (z,t)=\frac{2t-\cos y}{1-\sin x\cos y}+i\frac{1-2t\sin x}{1-\sin x\cos y}, \int_0^1 \psi (z,t) \, dt</math>
[[File:Virtual_tunnels.jpg|thumb|center|350px|Example 1: Virtual tunnels – Topographical (moduli) image of virtual integrals (one for each point) in the complex plane. [−10,10]]]

[[Image:Contours in the vector field f(z) = -Cos(z).jpg|thumb|right|350px|Two contours flowing towards an attractive fixed point (red on the left). The white contour (''c'' = 2) terminates before reaching the fixed point. The second contour (''c''(''n'') = square root of ''n'') terminates at the fixed point. For both contours, ''n'' = 10,000]]

'''Example.''' Let:

:<math>g_n(z)=z+\frac{c_n}{n}\phi  (z), \quad \text{with} \quad f(z) = z + \phi(z).</math>

Next, set <math>T_{1,n}(z)=g_n(z), T_{k,n}(z)= g_n(T_{k-1,n}(z)),</math> and ''T<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') = ''T<sub>n,n</sub>''(''z''). Let

:<math>T(z)=\lim_{n\to \infty} T_n(z)</math>

when that limit exists. The sequence {''T<sub>n</sub>''(''z'')} defines contours γ = γ(''c<sub>n</sub>'', ''z'') that follow the flow of the [[vector field]] ''f''(''z''). If there exists an attractive fixed point α, meaning |''f''(''z'') − α| ≤ ρ|''z'' − α| for 0 ≤ ρ < 1, then ''T<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') → ''T''(''z'') ≡ α along γ = γ(''c<sub>n</sub>'', ''z''), provided (for example) <math>c_n = \sqrt{n}</math>. If ''c<sub>n</sub>'' ≡ ''c'' > 0, then ''T<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') → ''T''(''z''), a point on the contour γ = γ(''c'', ''z''). It is easily seen that

:<math>\oint_\gamma \phi  (\zeta ) \, d\zeta =\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac c n \sum_{k=1}^n \phi ^2 \left (T_{k-1,n}(z) \right ) </math>

and

:<math>L(\gamma (z))=\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{c}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \left| \phi  \left (T_{k-1,n}(z) \right ) \right|, </math>

when these limits exist.

These concepts are marginally related to ''[[Active contour model|active contour theory]]'' in image processing, and are simple generalizations of the [[Euler method]]

=== Self-replicating expansions ===

====Series====
The series defined recursively by ''f<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') = ''z'' + ''g<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') have the property that the nth term is predicated on the sum of the first ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1 terms. In order to employ theorem (GF3) it is necessary to show boundedness in the following sense: If each ''f<sub>n</sub>'' is defined for |''z''| < ''M'' then |''G<sub>n</sub>''(''z'')| < ''M'' must follow before |''f<sub>n</sub>''(''z'')&nbsp;−&nbsp;''z''| =&nbsp;|''g<sub>n</sub>''(''z'')| ≤&nbsp;''Cβ<sub>n</sub>'' is defined for iterative purposes. This is because <math>g_n(G_{n-1}(z))</math> occurs throughout the expansion. The restriction

:<math>|z|<R=M-C\sum_{k=1}^\infty \beta_k >0</math>

serves this purpose. Then ''G<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') → ''G''(''z'') uniformly on the restricted domain.

'''Example (S1).'''   Set 
:<math>f_n(z)=z+\frac{1}{\rho n^2}\sqrt{z}, \qquad \rho >\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{6}}</math> 
and ''M'' = ρ<sup>2</sup>. Then ''R'' = ρ<sup>2</sup> − (π/6) > 0. Then, if <math>S=\left\{ z: |z|<R,\operatorname{Re}(z)>0 \right\}</math>, ''z'' in ''S'' implies |''G<sub>n</sub>''(''z'')| < ''M'' and theorem (GF3) applies, so that

:<math>\begin{align}
G_n(z) &=z+g_1(z)+g_2(G_1(z))+g_3(G_2(z))+\cdots + g_n(G_{n-1}(z)) \\ 
&= z+\frac{1}{\rho \cdot 1^2}\sqrt{z}+\frac{1}{\rho \cdot 2^2}\sqrt{G_1(z)}+\frac{1}{\rho \cdot 3^2}\sqrt{G_2(z)}+\cdots +\frac{1}{\rho \cdot n^2} \sqrt{G_{n-1}(z)}
\end{align}</math>

converges absolutely, hence is convergent.

'''Example (S2)''':   <math>f_n(z)=z+\frac 1 {n^2}\cdot \varphi (z), \varphi (z)=2\cos(x/y)+i2\sin (x/y), >G_n(z)=f_n \circ f_{n-1}\circ \cdots \circ f_1(z), \qquad [-10,10], n=50 </math>
[[File:Self-generating series3.jpg|thumb|center|325px|Example (S2)- A topographical (moduli) image of a self generating series.]]

====Products====
The product defined recursively by

:<math>f_n(z)=z( 1+g_n(z)), \qquad |z| \leqslant M,</math>

has the appearance

:<math>G_n(z) = z \prod _{k=1}^n \left( 1+g_k \left( G_{k-1}(z) \right) \right).</math>

In order to apply Theorem GF3 it is required that:

:<math>\left| zg_n(z) \right|\le C\beta_n, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^\infty \beta_k<\infty.</math>

Once again, a boundedness condition must support

:<math>\left|G_{n-1}(z) g_n(G_{n-1}(z))\right|\le C \beta_n.</math>

If one knows ''Cβ<sub>n</sub>'' in advance, the following will suffice:

:<math>|z| \leqslant R = \frac{M}{P} \qquad \text{where} \quad P = \prod_{n=1}^\infty \left( 1+C\beta_n\right).</math>

Then ''G<sub>n</sub>''(''z'') → ''G''(''z'') uniformly on the restricted domain.

'''Example (P1).'''  Suppose <math>f_n(z)=z(1+g_n(z))</math> with <math>g_n(z)=\tfrac{z^2}{n^3},</math> observing after a few preliminary computations, that |''z''| ≤ 1/4 implies |''G<sub>n</sub>''(''z'')| < 0.27. Then

:<math>\left|G_n(z)  \frac{G_n(z)^2}{n^3} \right|<(0.02)\frac{1}{n^3}=C\beta_n</math>

and

:<math>G_n(z)=z \prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left( 1+\frac{G_k(z)^2}{n^3}\right)</math>

converges uniformly.

'''Example (P2).'''

:<math>g_{k,n}(z)=z\left( 1+\frac 1 n \varphi \left (z,\tfrac k n \right ) \right),</math> 
:<math>G_{n,n}(z)= \left( g_{n,n}\circ g_{n-1,n}\circ \cdots \circ g_{1,n} \right ) (z) = z\prod_{k=1}^n ( 1+P_{k,n}(z)),</math>
:<math>P_{k,n}(z)=\frac 1 n \varphi \left (G_{k-1,n}(z),\tfrac{k}{n} \right ),</math>
:<math>\prod_{k=1}^{n-1} \left( 1+P_{k,n}(z) \right) = 1+P_{1,n}(z)+P_{2,n}(z)+\cdots + P_{k-1,n}(z) + R_n(z) \sim \int_0^1 \pi (z,t) \, dt + 1+R_n(z),</math>
:<math>\varphi (z)=x\cos(y)+iy\sin(x), \int_0^1 (z\pi (z,t)-1) \,dt, \qquad [-15,15]: </math>

[[Image:Picasso's Universe.jpg|thumb|center|350px|Example (P2): Picasso's Universe – a derived virtual integral from a self-generating infinite product. Click on image for higher resolution.]]

====Continued fractions====
'''Example (CF1)''': A self-generating continued fraction.<ref name=Gillc />

: <math>\begin{align}
F_n(z) &= \frac{\rho (z)}{\delta_1+} \frac{\rho (F_1(z))}{\delta_2 +} \frac{\rho (F_2(z))}{\delta_3+} \cdots \frac{\rho (F_{n-1}(z))}{\delta_n}, \\
\rho (z) &= \frac{\cos(y)}{\cos (y)+\sin (x)}+i\frac{\sin(x)}{\cos (y)+\sin (x)}, \qquad [0<x<20],[0<y<20], \qquad\delta_k\equiv 1
\end{align}</math>

[[Image:Diminishing returns.jpg|thumb|center|350px|Example CF1: Diminishing returns – a topographical (moduli) image of a self-generating continued fraction.]]

'''Example (CF2)''': Best described as a self-generating reverse [[Euler's continued fraction formula|Euler continued fraction]].<ref name=Gillc />

: <math>G_n(z)=\frac{\rho (G_{n-1}(z))}{1+\rho (G_{n-1}(z))-}\ \frac{\rho (G_{n-2}(z))}{1+\rho (G_{n-2}(z))-}\cdots \frac{\rho (G_1(z))}{1+\rho (G_1(z))-}\ \frac{\rho (z)}{1+\rho (z)-z},</math> 
:<math>\rho (z)=\rho (x+iy)=x\cos(y)+iy\sin(x), \qquad [-15,15], n=30 </math>

[[Image:Dream of Gold.jpg|thumb|center|350px|Example CF2: Dream of Gold – a topographical (moduli) image of a self-generating reverse Euler continued fraction.]]
